# WAF, Shield, Firewall Manager and Network Firewall: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=edge-protection-q004 -->
### Question 1

A company protects its sign-in page with an AWS WAF web ACL on an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The sign-in page is part of the company's own web application. The web ACL has a rate-based rule that limits each IP address. Attackers now try stolen user names and passwords from thousands of IP addresses, and each address sends a few requests each hour. Real users must keep signing in during the attack. The company must ensure that requests with stolen credentials are stopped. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Lower the request limit of the existing rate-based rule so that each IP address can send fewer sign-in requests.
- Add a rate-based rule with a scope-down statement for the sign-in page that counts all requests and blocks them above a limit.
- Export the AWS WAF logs each day, build an IP set of the addresses that failed to sign in, and block that IP set.
- Add the AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention managed rule group to the web ACL, and point it at the sign-in endpoint.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add the AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention managed rule group to the web ACL, and point it at the sign-in endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "stolen user names and passwords", "from thousands of IP addresses", "Real users must keep signing in", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead, and the sentence before it asks me to ensure that requests with stolen credentials are stopped.
2. I mark the constraints: stolen user names and passwords, thousands of IP addresses, a few requests from each address, and real users must keep signing in.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a managed rule group that checks the credentials themselves, because each address stays under a per-address limit.
4. I remove the lower limit on the existing rule, because the rule counts each IP address on its own and every attacking address stays far below it. I remove the daily IP set, because it is a day late and the team rebuilds it by hand.
5. Between the scope-down rule with Count all and the account takeover prevention rule group the difference is who gets blocked; the stem says real users must keep signing in, so a limit on all sign-in requests fails when the attack pushes the total above it.
6. Check: the account takeover prevention rule group inspects login attempts, compares them with a stolen credential database, and needs no list from the team. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Each address stays below a per-address limit, so request counting misses the attack. The account takeover prevention (ATP) managed rule group works by [inspecting login attempts](../facts/waf.md#waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts) and checks them [against its stolen credential database](../facts/waf.md#waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts). It acts on the credentials, not on the request rate, so real users keep signing in.

**Why not.**

- "Lower the request limit of the existing rate-based ...": The rule counts each address separately, [based on the request IP address](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-default-key-ip), and each attacking address stays far below a limit that real users can reach.
- "Add a rate-based rule with a scope-down statement ...": [A rate-based rule with a scope-down statement](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-scope-down) and Count all limits the sign-in requests together, so real users are blocked too when the total passes the limit.
- "Export the AWS WAF logs each day, build ...": A daily IP set is a day behind thousands of changing addresses, and the team rebuilds the set by hand each day.

**Twin.** If the stem said "from a few IP addresses that each send thousands of requests" instead: the existing rate-based rule works, because new requests stay blocked until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls).

**Takeaway.** Stolen passwords from many addresses: the ATP managed rule group, not a lower per-address limit.

**Review.** [A rate-based rule limits each key that sends requests too fast](2-deep.md#a-rate-based-rule-limits-each-key-that-sends-requests-too-fast-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances reach the internet through NAT gateways. The operations team is small and does not write its own detection rules. Attackers send requests that contain SQL injection code to the application. The company must block these requests. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with the Application Load Balancer.
- Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, and route the private subnets' traffic through the firewall endpoints.
- Add security group rules and network ACL rules that inspect the domain names and the content of the traffic.
- Run proxy software on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that inspects every inbound request and every outbound connection.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with the Application Load Balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "requests that contain SQL injection code", "does not write its own detection rules", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** SQL injection code arrives inside HTTP requests, so the control reads each request at the load balancer. AWS and AWS Marketplace sellers [automatically update managed rule groups](../facts/waf.md#waf-managed-rules-auto-updated) when new threats emerge, so the small team writes no rules and runs no extra instances.

**Why not.**

- "Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain ...": A domain list rule group looks for domain names in the [Server Name Indication (SNI) extension](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header) or the host header, so it does not read SQL injection code.
- "Add security group rules and network ACL rules ...": Security groups and network ACLs give [traffic control at a Layer 4 level (IP address and port ranges)](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services), so they do not read request content.
- "Run proxy software on a fleet of Amazon ...": It can work, but the team builds, patches and scales a proxy fleet and writes its rules, which is far more work than a managed rule group.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The instances must reach only an approved list of software update domains" instead: AWS Network Firewall, because it supports [allow lists and deny lists with domain names](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-allow-deny-lists).

**Takeaway.** Attack code inside web requests: a web ACL with managed rule groups on the load balancer.

**Review.** [A web ACL checks each HTTP request against its rules in priority order](2-deep.md#a-web-acl-checks-each-http-request-against-its-rules-in-priority-order-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company serves a login page through an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of an Application Load Balancer. Each minute, the page receives thousands of requests from a small set of IP addresses. The set of addresses changes every few hours. Real users send a few requests each. The company must stop the flood as soon as possible without blocking real users. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Add network ACL deny rules for the attacking IP addresses to the load balancer subnets, and update the rules when the addresses change.
- Add a rate-based rule to a web ACL on the CloudFront distribution that blocks each IP address above a request limit.
- Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and ask the Shield Response Team to block the attacking IP addresses during each attack.
- Add inbound deny rules for the attacking IP addresses to the security group of the load balancer, and update them when the addresses change.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Add a rate-based rule to a web ACL on the CloudFront distribution that blocks each IP address above a request limit.

**Deciding phrases.** "a small set of IP addresses", "changes every few hours", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** A few addresses send many requests, which is the case that rate-based rules handle: AWS designs them for [brute force login attempts](../facts/waf.md#waf-faq-rate-based-web-layer-ddos). After an address passes the limit, its new requests are blocked until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls). The rule follows the changing addresses by itself, and real users stay under the limit.

**Why not.**

- "Add network ACL deny rules for the attacking ...": The addresses change every few hours, so someone edits the rules by hand, and a network ACL has [20 rules per network ACL](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-quota-rules-per-network-acl) by default.
- "Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and ask the ...": It can help, but Shield Advanced needs a [1-year subscription commitment](../facts/shield.md#shield-advanced-one-year-commitment) and a monthly fee, which costs far more than one rate-based rule.
- "Add inbound deny rules for the attacking IP ...": In a security group, [you can specify allow rules, but not deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only), so the deny list does not exist.

**Twin.** If the stem said "thousands of IP addresses that each try a few stolen passwords" instead: a per-address limit misses them, so add the account takeover prevention rule group, which works by [inspecting login attempts](../facts/waf.md#waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts).

**Takeaway.** A few addresses that send too many requests: a rate-based rule in the web ACL.

**Review.** [A rate-based rule limits each key that sends requests too fast](2-deep.md#a-rate-based-rule-limits-each-key-that-sends-requests-too-fast-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and adds new member accounts every month. The accounts run Application Load Balancers in two AWS Regions and Amazon CloudFront distributions. The security team must centrally manage one set of AWS WAF rules for every load balancer and every distribution, including the resources in new accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Write a script that runs each day in every account, creates a web ACL in each Region, and associates it with each new resource.
- Turn on AWS Firewall Manager separately in each account, and create one AWS WAF policy in each account that covers all Regions.
- Subscribe the organization to AWS Shield Advanced so that AWS applies web exploit rules to the resources in every account automatically.
- Enable AWS Config, set a Firewall Manager administrator account, and create a Global AWS WAF policy plus one per Region with load balancers.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable AWS Config, set a Firewall Manager administrator account, and create a Global AWS WAF policy plus one per Region with load balancers.

**Deciding phrases.** "adds new member accounts every month", "centrally manage", "two AWS Regions", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Firewall Manager lets you [centrally configure and manage firewall rules](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-definition-central-rules) across the organization, and in a new account [Firewall Manager automatically applies the policy](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts). It also needs AWS Config: [you must enable AWS Config](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-requires-aws-config). CloudFront distributions use one Global policy, and load balancers need [separate Firewall Manager policies for each Region](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-waf-policy-global-for-cloudfront).

**Why not.**

- "Write a script that runs each day in ...": It can work, but the team maintains a script in every account and Region, which is more work than one managed policy.
- "Turn on AWS Firewall Manager separately in each ...": Firewall Manager runs from [the Firewall Manager administrator account](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-faq-prereq-administrator-account), and [security policies are region specific](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-policies-region-specific), so one policy does not cover all Regions.
- "Subscribe the organization to AWS Shield Advanced so ...": Shield Advanced is DDoS protection, and AWS Shield [does not inspect the contents](../facts/shield.md#shield-no-http-content-inspection) of HTTP requests, so it adds no web exploit rules.

**Twin.** If the stem said "one account with one load balancer" instead: associate one web ACL with the load balancer directly, because Firewall Manager suits cases where you [protect your entire organization](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-best-for-whole-org).

**Takeaway.** The same AWS WAF rules in every account, new ones too: Firewall Manager AWS WAF policies.

**Review.** [Firewall Manager applies the same protections to every account in an organization](2-deep.md#firewall-manager-applies-the-same-protections-to-every-account-in-an-organization-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company serves a web application from Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets across two Availability Zones. A Network Load Balancer receives the HTTP requests from users on the internet and forwards them to the instances. The security team must block common web exploits, such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups directly with the existing Network Load Balancer.
- Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the Elastic IP addresses of the Network Load Balancer as protected resources.
- Move the traffic to an Application Load Balancer, and associate a web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with it.
- Install an open source web application firewall on each EC2 instance, and update its detection rules from a public feed every week.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Move the traffic to an Application Load Balancer, and associate a web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with it.

**Deciding phrases.** "A Network Load Balancer receives the HTTP requests", "block common web exploits", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS WAF reads web requests on regional services such as an Application Load Balancer, where [your rules run in region](../facts/waf.md#waf-regional-rules-run-in-region-internal). The list of resource types for a web ACL does not name a Network Load Balancer, so the traffic moves to an Application Load Balancer. Managed rule groups are rules that [AWS and AWS Marketplace sellers write and maintain](../facts/waf.md#waf-managed-rule-groups-definition), and the core rule set is [generally applicable to web applications](../facts/waf.md#waf-core-rule-set-owasp).

**Why not.**

- "Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses ...": The list of resources that a web ACL protects names [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types) and others, and it does not name a Network Load Balancer.
- "Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the ...": Shield Advanced protects against DDoS floods, but AWS Shield [does not inspect the contents](../facts/shield.md#shield-no-http-content-inspection) of HTTP requests, so SQL injection code passes.
- "Install an open source web application firewall on ...": It can work, but the team installs, patches and updates software on every instance, which is far more work than a managed web ACL.

**Twin.** If the stem said "behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution" instead: associate the web ACL with the distribution, because AWS WAF is [available globally for CloudFront distributions](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1).

**Takeaway.** A web ACL protects an Application Load Balancer; its list of resource types does not name a Network Load Balancer.

**Review.** [Each resource has one web ACL in the same Region as the resource](2-deep.md#each-resource-has-one-web-acl-in-the-same-region-as-the-resource-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=edge-protection-q005 -->
### Question 6

A company runs an internet-facing web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer. The instances reach the internet through NAT gateways. The operations team is small and does not write its own detection rules. A review finds that the instances can download files from any domain on the internet. The instances must reach only an approved list of software update domains. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses AWS managed rule groups with the Application Load Balancer.
- Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, and route the private subnets' traffic through the firewall endpoints.
- Add security group rules and network ACL rules that inspect the domain names and the content of the traffic.
- Run proxy software on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that inspects every inbound request and every outbound connection.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Deploy AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, and route the private subnets' traffic through the firewall endpoints.

**Deciding phrases.** "download files from any domain on the internet", "an approved list of software update domains", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The outbound connections leave the VPC, so the control sits in their route. Network Firewall supports [allow lists and deny lists with domain names](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-allow-deny-lists), and for HTTPS it reads the [Server Name Indication (SNI) extension](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-domain-sni-host-header). Protection starts after [you modify your Amazon VPC route tables](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection) so that the private subnets' traffic goes through the firewall endpoints.

**Why not.**

- "Associate an AWS WAF web ACL that uses ...": A web ACL on the load balancer reads requests that arrive at the load balancer; the instances' outbound connections leave through the NAT gateways and do not pass the web ACL.
- "Add security group rules and network ACL rules ...": Security groups and network ACLs give [traffic control at a Layer 4 level (IP address and port ranges)](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-sec05-finer-control-services), so they do not read domain names.
- "Run proxy software on a fleet of Amazon ...": It can work, but the team builds, patches and scales a proxy fleet and writes its rules, which is far more work than a managed firewall.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Attackers send requests that contain SQL injection code to the application" instead: a web ACL with managed rule groups, because they block patterns [like SQL injection attacks](../facts/waf.md#waf-sql-database-group).

**Takeaway.** Outbound traffic to approved domains: Network Firewall with a domain list, in the route of the traffic.

**Review.** [Network Firewall inspects VPC traffic only when route tables send it there](2-deep.md#network-firewall-inspects-vpc-traffic-only-when-route-tables-send-it-there-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs a mission-critical web application behind an Amazon CloudFront distribution and an Application Load Balancer. The company has an AWS Enterprise Support plan. During a DDoS attack, the company must get help from AWS DDoS experts at any hour. The company also must be able to request a credit for the scaling charges that an attack causes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Rely on AWS Shield Standard, and open an AWS Support case to request DDoS help and a billing refund during each attack.
- Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the distribution and the load balancer as protected resources after an attack starts.
- Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now, and protect both resources, each with a web ACL that has a rate-based rule in Block mode.
- Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now, protect both resources with rate-based rules, and place AWS Network Firewall endpoints in front of the load balancer.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now, and protect both resources, each with a web ACL that has a rate-based rule in Block mode.

**Deciding phrases.** "help from AWS DDoS experts at any hour", "request a credit for the scaling charges", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Shield Advanced adds [24/7 support from the Shield Response Team](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection), and after an attack you can [request a Shield Advanced service credit](../facts/shield.md#shield-cost-protection-credit) for the extra charges. Resources [added during an attack are not eligible](../facts/shield.md#shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack), so both resources are protected now, each with a rate-based rule [in the web ACL in Block mode](../facts/shield.md#shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack).

**Why not.**

- "Rely on AWS Shield Standard, and open an ...": The response team and cost protection come with Shield Advanced, which adds [24/7 support from the Shield Response Team](../facts/shield.md#shield-faq-advanced-layers-srt-cost-protection); Shield Standard is the automatic basic layer.
- "Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced, and add the ...": Resources [added during an attack are not eligible](../facts/shield.md#shield-credit-prereqs-before-attack) for a credit, so the company loses cost protection for the attack that is already running.
- "Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced now, protect both ...": The Shield part works, but the endpoints add work, and Network Firewall is designed for VPC access control, [but not to mitigate volumetric attacks](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-not-for-ddos).

**Twin.** If the stem said "must keep costs low and needs no DDoS experts" instead: Shield Standard with AWS WAF rate-based rules, because Shield Standard comes [at no additional charge](../facts/shield.md#shield-standard-automatic-no-charge).

**Takeaway.** DDoS experts and cost credits: Shield Advanced, with protection and a Block rate rule in place before the attack.

**Review.** [Shield Standard protects every account free but Shield Advanced adds paid response](2-deep.md#shield-standard-protects-every-account-free-but-shield-advanced-adds-paid-response-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company's developers work in the Europe (Ireland) Region. A developer creates an AWS WAF web ACL and an IP set in Europe (Ireland) to block a list of addresses. The web ACL must protect an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The origin of the distribution is an Application Load Balancer in US West (Oregon). When the developer tries to associate the web ACL, the distribution does not appear in the list of resources. What should the developer do?

- Create the web ACL and the IP set again in US East (N. Virginia), and associate the web ACL with the distribution.
- Associate the IP set directly with the distribution, and keep the web ACL in Europe (Ireland) for later use.
- Create the web ACL and the IP set again in US West (Oregon), the origin's Region, and associate the web ACL there.
- Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the distribution first, so that the distribution appears in the list of web ACL resources.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create the web ACL and the IP set again in US East (N. Virginia), and associate the web ACL with the distribution.

**Deciding phrases.** "an IP set in Europe (Ireland)", "protect an Amazon CloudFront distribution"

**Why.** AWS WAF is [available globally for CloudFront distributions](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1), but you [use the Region US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1) to create the web ACL and the resources that it uses. An IP set for such a web ACL is created in the Global scope as well: [you must use Global (CloudFront)](../facts/waf.md#waf-ip-set-global-for-cloudfront).

**Why not.**

- "Associate the IP set directly with the distribution, ...": In a rule, [you reference the set](../facts/waf.md#waf-ip-set-collection-of-addresses) through an IP set statement; an IP set is not associated with a resource on its own.
- "Create the web ACL and the IP set ...": The origin's Region does not decide it: a web ACL goes in [the Region where the associated resource is located](../facts/waf.md#waf-web-acl-region-of-resource), and for a distribution that is [US East (N. Virginia)](../facts/waf.md#waf-web-acl-region-of-resource).
- "Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the distribution first, ...": Shield Advanced is DDoS protection and does not change where a web ACL for CloudFront is created; AWS WAF is [available globally for CloudFront distributions](../facts/waf.md#waf-cloudfront-web-acl-us-east-1).

**Twin.** If the stem said "must protect the Application Load Balancer" instead: create the web ACL in US West (Oregon), [the Region where the associated resource is located](../facts/waf.md#waf-web-acl-region-of-resource).

**Takeaway.** A web ACL for CloudFront and its IP sets are created in US East (N. Virginia), whatever the origin Region.

**Review.** [Each resource has one web ACL in the same Region as the resource](2-deep.md#each-resource-has-one-web-acl-in-the-same-region-as-the-resource-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs workloads in private subnets across multiple Availability Zones of one VPC. The VPC has public subnets and a NAT gateway in each of its three zones. All traffic between the internet and the workloads must be inspected by AWS Network Firewall. The inspection must continue if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST resilient way? (Select TWO.)

- Create a dedicated firewall subnet in each Availability Zone, and place one firewall endpoint in each of these subnets.
- Create one firewall endpoint in a single Availability Zone, and route the traffic of all three zones through that endpoint.
- Place the firewall endpoints in the same subnets as the workloads, so that no extra subnets are needed in the VPC.
- Update the route tables so that the traffic of each zone goes in both directions through the firewall endpoint in that same zone.
- Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the internet gateway, and add rule groups that inspect all inbound and outbound packets.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a dedicated firewall subnet in each Availability Zone, and place one firewall endpoint in each of these subnets.
- Update the route tables so that the traffic of each zone goes in both directions through the firewall endpoint in that same zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "inspected by AWS Network Firewall", "if one Availability Zone fails", "MOST resilient"

**Why.** Firewall endpoints are installed [on a per-Availability Zone basis](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoints-per-az), each in [a dedicated subnet](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-faq-dedicated-subnet-28). Incoming traffic goes to [the firewall in the same Availability Zone](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-two-az-same-zone-routing) as its subnet, so one zone failure stops one endpoint, not all inspection.

- Each zone gets [a subnet to host the primary firewall endpoint](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoints-per-az), so a zone failure removes one endpoint and the other zones keep their inspection.
- Same-zone routing sends each flow through [the Network Firewall endpoint in both directions](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-no-asymmetric-routing), and a zone failure leaves the routes of the other zones intact.

**Why not.**

- "Create one firewall endpoint in a single Availability ...": It inspects the traffic, but one endpoint in one zone is a single point of failure for all three zones, which is the least resilient design.
- "Place the firewall endpoints in the same subnets ...": An endpoint protects subnets [except for the one in which it's located](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoint-not-own-subnet), so workloads in its own subnet are not inspected.
- "Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the ...": A web ACL protects resources such as [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types); an internet gateway is not in that list.

**Twin.** If the stem said "in one Availability Zone" instead: one firewall subnet and one endpoint are enough, because endpoints are installed [on a per-Availability Zone basis](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-endpoints-per-az).

**Takeaway.** Network Firewall across zones: one endpoint in a dedicated subnet per zone, and same-zone routes both ways.

**Review.** [Network Firewall inspects VPC traffic only when route tables send it there](2-deep.md#network-firewall-inspects-vpc-traffic-only-when-route-tables-send-it-there-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company has many AWS accounts in AWS Organizations with all features enabled. AWS Config is enabled in every account. A review finds security groups that allow SSH on port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. From a single location, the security team must audit the security group rules in every account, including new accounts, and must fix such rules automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an AWS WAF web ACL in every account with a rule that blocks port 22, and associate it with each EC2 instance.
- Deploy AWS Network Firewall in each VPC with a stateless rule that drops traffic to port 22 from any address.
- Create an AWS Firewall Manager security group policy that checks rule content and remediates noncompliant rules, scoped to the organization.
- Write an AWS Lambda function in each account that scans security groups each hour and deletes rules that allow SSH from any address.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an AWS Firewall Manager security group policy that checks rule content and remediates noncompliant rules, scoped to the organization.

**Deciding phrases.** "From a single location", "including new accounts", "fix such rules automatically", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A Firewall Manager security group policy can [Audit security group rules](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-sg-policy-three-uses) to find and fix noncompliant rules, and a policy can [automatically remediate noncompliant resources](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-audit-or-auto-remediate). In a new account, [Firewall Manager automatically applies the policy](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-auto-applies-to-new-accounts), so the team writes no code for each account.

**Why not.**

- "Create an AWS WAF web ACL in every ...": A web ACL protects resources such as [Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway, Application Load Balancer](../facts/waf.md#waf-protected-resource-types); an EC2 instance is not in that list, and a web ACL does not change security group rules.
- "Deploy AWS Network Firewall in each VPC with ...": Network Firewall filters the traffic that route tables send [through the Network Firewall firewall endpoints](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-route-tables-enable-protection), and the open security group rules stay in place.
- "Write an AWS Lambda function in each account ...": It can work, but the team writes, deploys and maintains code in every account, including each new account, which a managed policy avoids.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must report the open rules without changing them" instead: the same policy type that lists noncompliant resources [without taking corrective action](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-audit-or-auto-remediate).

**Takeaway.** Find and fix risky security group rules in every account: a Firewall Manager security group policy.

**Review.** [Firewall Manager applies the same protections to every account in an organization](2-deep.md#firewall-manager-applies-the-same-protections-to-every-account-in-an-organization-3-min)

</details>
